messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
Bao, at eighty years old, still approached the world with the meticulous logic of the data scientist he had been his entire life. He believed in patterns, in predictable systems, and in the quiet order of a well-structured database. It was a worldview that had been shattered thirty years ago in a dusty, sun-scorched checkpoint outside a city under siege, and the chaos of that day had been corrupting his personal code ever since. He had been part of a relief convoy, his role to manage the logistics of aid distribution. They were stopped for hours, penned in by jumpy, teenage soldiers on one side and a desperate crowd of civilians on the other. He remembers the feeling of absolute paralysis, of having no options as the soldiers swaggered and the people pleaded. This sensation of being trapped was the first crack in his foundation. What broke him, however, was a smaller, more intimate horror. While the soldiers extorted medical supplies, he watched a man claw a food packet from the hands of an elderly woman in the crowd, shoving her to the ground. In that moment, surrounded by the larger violence of war, it was this act of casual cruelty—this profound misbehavior—that filled him with a rage so pure and helpless it felt like it would incinerate him from the inside. He could do nothing.

In the years that followed his return to the States, the event did not fade into the past. Instead, it remained terrifyingly present. Bao would be sitting in his armchair when, without warning, the memory would unspool not as a recollection but as a live feed. He would feel the searing heat on his skin, taste the grit of dust in his mouth, and hear the frantic shouting as if it were happening right now, outside his window. He described it to himself as a film that plays over and over, a reel he could not stop. Even sleep offered no escape. He would often wake in the pre-dawn darkness, his heart hammering against his ribs, the phantom sensation of grit in his mouth and the suffocating heat of the dream still clinging to him like a shroud. For several long minutes after waking, his familiar bedroom would feel alien, its quiet safety failing to penetrate the vivid afterimage of the checkpoint. His body, too, refused to believe it was over; it remained constantly tense, a coiled spring perpetually ready to react to a danger that his rational mind knew was gone. This constant state of being on alert was exhausting, a low-grade hum of dread that underscored every moment. He found himself scanning every room he entered, noting exits, assessing the faces of strangers in the grocery aisle for any sign of aggression. The world, which he had once navigated with calm assurance, had become a landscape of latent threats.

Over the decades, Bao built a fortress of routines to protect himself. He stopped watching the news entirely; any report of conflict, no matter how distant, felt like a personal summons back to that checkpoint. His relationships grew strained. His grandchildren learned that sudden noises or arguments would send their quiet, gentle grandfather into a state of sharp, inexplicable irritability. After one particularly harsh outburst at his grandson for a minor squabble, a deep fear took root in Bao’s mind: he was terrified that he would not be able to control his anger and would do something terrible. This fear led him to rehearse what to say before any interaction, practicing calm, neutral phrases in the mirror to preempt a rage he felt simmering just beneath his skin. This internal battle, the stark contrast between his logical self and the volatile stranger who now seemed to live inside him, fed his most persistent and terrifying belief: that his reactions meant he was going crazy. The intrusive, vivid memories and the uncontainable anger were not symptoms of trauma, he was certain, but proof that his mind was fundamentally breaking.

The decision to seek help came after an incident in his apartment building. The elevator shuddered to a halt between floors, trapping him alone in the small, humming box. The sudden loss of control, the feeling of having no options, was an exact replica of the helplessness he’d felt at the checkpoint. The metal walls seemed to press in, the air grew thick and hot, and he was no longer in an elevator in Chicago but back in the convoy, suffocating on dust and rage. When the doors finally opened, a neighbor found him drenched in sweat, gasping for air. The public exposure of his private terror was the final piece of data he needed. Bao came to therapy not with a desire to talk about the war, but with the quiet, desperate plea of a man of logic who fears his own internal system has become irrevocably corrupted and dangerous.
